title: Compact probability kernels approximate the identity in L2
statement: Use $\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field]. Let $m\geq1$ and $r\geq0$ be integers and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbf R^m$. Let $k:\mathbf R^m\to\mathbf R$ be measurable, nonnegative almost everywhere, integrable, with $\int k=1$, and zero almost everywhere outside the closed unit ball. For $\epsilon>0$ define $k_\epsilon(y)=\epsilon^{-m}k(y/\epsilon)$. For each measurable $g:\mathbf R^m\to\mathbf R^r$ with $\int\|g\|^2<\infty$, the convolution $$A_\epsilon g(x)=\int_{\mathbf R^m}k_\epsilon(y)g(x-y)\,dy$$ exists for almost every $x$, represents an element of $L^2$ (measurable functions modulo almost-everywhere equality), and satisfies $\|A_\epsilon g\|_2\leq\|g\|_2$ and $$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\|A_\epsilon g-g\|_2=0,\qquad\|g\|_2=\left(\int\|g(x)\|^2\,dx\right)^{1/2}.$$ The resulting $L^2$ class is independent of the measurable representatives of $k$ and $g$.

proof.text: First choose Borel representatives of $k,g$ using [lem-sfb-euclidean-bochner-integral-calculus]. Replace the representative of $k$ by its nonnegative part times the indicator of the closed unit ball; this is Borel, equals $k$ almost everywhere, and is everywhere nonnegative and zero outside that ball. These replacements preserve the hypotheses. For any fixed $x$, the map $y\mapsto x-y$ preserves null sets: every null set lies in a Borel null set $B$, and [lem-sfb-euclidean-jacobian-nonnegative-integrability], applied to this global affine diffeomorphism, whose absolute Jacobian is $1$, and to the indicator of $B$, gives that the Borel preimage of $B$ has measure $\int\mathbf 1_B=0$. The same argument for $y\mapsto y/\epsilon$ has constant positive Jacobian $\epsilon^{-m}$ and also preserves null sets. Thus for every fixed $\epsilon>0$ and $x$, replacing $k,g$ by these representatives changes the integrand only on a null set in $y$. The integrability and integral clauses of [lem-sfb-euclidean-bochner-integral-calculus] then show that all section integrals, wherever integrable, agree. We may prove the assertions for these Borel representatives. This also establishes independence of the original representatives once existence has been proved.

proof.text: Fix $\epsilon>0$ and put $h(y)=k_\epsilon(y)$. It is Borel and nonnegative and vanishes for $\|y\|>\epsilon$. In [lem-sfb-euclidean-jacobian-nonnegative-integrability] take $D=D'=S=\mathbf R^m$ and $F(y)=y/\epsilon$, with absolute Jacobian $\epsilon^{-m}$. The nonnegative formula gives $\int h=\int k=1$, and the integrability clause gives integrability of $h$. The elementary support calculation is $\|y/\epsilon\|=\|y\|/\epsilon$. All change-of-variable maps here are globally bijective $C^1$ maps with $C^1$ inverse, as required.

proof.text: Define the possibly infinite nonnegative integral $H(x)=\int h(y)\|g(x-y)\|^2\,dy$. Its joint integrand is Borel: subtraction is continuous, $g,h$ are Borel, and products and squared norms preserve measurability. By [lem-sfb-tonelli-nonnegative-product] its iterated integrals can be swapped. Translation $x\mapsto x-y$ has absolute Jacobian $1$, so [lem-sfb-euclidean-jacobian-nonnegative-integrability] gives $\int\|g(x-y)\|^2\,dx=\|g\|_2^2$. Consequently $\int H(x)\,dx=\int h(y)\|g\|_2^2\,dy=\|g\|_2^2<\infty$. The finite-integral clause of [lem-sfb-tonelli-nonnegative-product] gives $H(x)<\infty$ for almost every $x$.

source.place: Agent assembly using the additive translation-continuity instance at 53–59, the Bochner/Prod integration facts and Jacobian change of variables identified by the cited nodes; not a proof quoted from this file.

proof.text: For each $x$ with $H(x)<\infty$, apply the scalar integral Cauchy–Schwarz clause of [lem-sfb-real-l2-hilbert-pairing] to $a(y)=\sqrt{h(y)}$ and $b(y)=\sqrt{h(y)}\|g(x-y)\|$. Both are measurable and square integrable, with squared norm integrals $1$ and $H(x)$. It gives $\int h(y)\|g(x-y)\|\,dy\leq\sqrt{H(x)}<\infty$. The norm criterion of [lem-sfb-euclidean-bochner-integral-calculus] proves existence of the required vector integral at this $x$; its norm bound gives $\|A_\epsilon g(x)\|^2\leq H(x)$.

proof.text: Apply the parameter-integral measurability clause of [lem-sfb-euclidean-bochner-integral-calculus] to the Borel function $(x,y)\mapsto h(y)g(x-y)$; assign zero to a nonintegrable section. This produces a Borel representative of $A_\epsilon g$. Integrating the preceding nonnegative inequality, using monotonicity from [lem-sfb-tonelli-nonnegative-product], gives $\int\|A_\epsilon g\|^2\leq\int H=\|g\|_2^2$. It therefore defines an $L^2$ class with the claimed contraction bound. By step 1 this is also the class for every original measurable representative.

proof.text:
Linearity from [lem-sfb-euclidean-bochner-integral-calculus] and $\int h=1$ give $A_\epsilon g(x)-g(x)=\int h(y)(g(x-y)-g(x))\,dy$ for almost every $x$: both original sections are integrable, the constant-vector section having norm integral $\|g(x)\|$. Put $H_\Delta(x)=\int h(y)\|g(x-y)-g(x)\|^2\,dy$. Tonelli [lem-sfb-tonelli-nonnegative-product] and $\|u-v\|^2\leq2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2$ give $\int H_\Delta\leq4\|g\|_2^2$, using the unit-Jacobian translation formula of [lem-sfb-euclidean-jacobian-nonnegative-integrability]. Hence $H_\Delta<\infty$ almost everywhere. For those $x$, Cauchy–Schwarz [lem-sfb-real-l2-hilbert-pairing] with $\sqrt h$ and $\sqrt h\|g(x-y)-g(x)\|$, followed by the Bochner norm bound, gives $\|A_\epsilon g(x)-g(x)\|^2\leq H_\Delta(x)$. Integrate and swap the nonnegative integrals to obtain
$$\|A_\epsilon g-g\|_2^2\leq\int h(y)\|T_y g-g\|_2^2\,dy,\qquad T_y g(x)=g(x-y).$$
All the integrands are Borel before integration, and Lebesgue measure on each Euclidean factor is sigma-finite.

proof.text: Given $\eta>0$, [lem-sfb-l2-translation-continuity] supplies $\delta>0$ such that $\|T_y g-g\|_2<\eta/2$ for $\|y\|<\delta$. If $0<\epsilon<\delta$, $h$ vanishes outside $\|y\|\leq\epsilon$, so monotonicity and scalar homogeneity [lem-sfb-tonelli-nonnegative-product] bound the last integral by $(\eta/2)^2\int h=(\eta/2)^2$. Thus $\|A_\epsilon g-g\|_2\leq\eta/2<\eta$, proving the asserted right-hand limit. The argument also covers $g=0$ and $r=0$, since all squared norms and integrals then vanish.
